true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `self.downsize` method definition silently overrides the width/height variant

Two class methods named `downsize` are defined: one accepting `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` (line 145) and a second accepting `(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` (line 149). Ruby allows method redefinition, so the second definition completely replaces the first — the width/height variant becomes dead code and unreachable. Any existing caller elsewhere in the codebase that still invokes `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, width, height, opts)` with 5 positional arguments will now raise an ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments) because the active method only accepts 3 positional args plus an options hash. This is an undocumented, breaking change to the public API of `OptimizedImage.downsize` and the first definition should be removed or the overload properly consolidated.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10MB client-side file size limit ignores per-type SiteSettings

`validateUploadedFile` previously computed `maxSizeKB` from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, allowing separate configurable limits for images vs attachments. It now hardcodes `10 * 1024` KB for all upload types, so admin-configured `max_image_size_kb`/`max_attachment_size_kb` settings are no longer respected client-side. This creates an inconsistency with server-side logic (uploads_controller.rb) which still consults `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`, and silently changes the enforced limit for attachments regardless of what the admin configured.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error handler reports a hardcoded 10MB limit instead of the configured value

In `displayErrorForUpload`, the 413 (entity too large) handler now hardcodes `maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024` instead of reading `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`. The error message shown to the user will state an incorrect maximum size whenever the site is configured with a different `max_image_size_kb` value, misleading users about the actual upload limit.

Hardcoded 10MB download cap ignores SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb

The API URL-download path now uses a hardcoded `10.megabytes` limit instead of the configurable `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` that was previously used. This removes admin control over the maximum download size for API-sourced uploads (both images and non-image attachments go through this code path), and is inconsistent with the newly-added downsizing logic a few lines below that still reads `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` to decide when to shrink an image. Admins who configure a smaller max image/attachment size will no longer have that limit enforced for URL-based uploads.

In-place downsizing with identical from/to path risks data corruption and silent oversized uploads

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` uses the same path for both source and destination. For animated GIFs this is routed to `gifsicle --output <path>` with the same input and output path (see `resize_instructions_animated`/`downsize_instructions_animated` in optimized_image.rb); depending on how gifsicle buffers input before writing, this can truncate/corrupt the source file while it is still being read. Additionally, if `OptimizedImage.downsize` fails (returns false, e.g., ImageMagick/gifsicle missing or erroring) the loop still decrements `attempt` without any error reported to the user, and if the file is still over the limit after 5 attempts, the upload proceeds silently with the oversized file instead of surfacing an error to the caller.

No test coverage for the new automatic image downsizing feature

The PR adds a non-trivial feature — automatically downsizing images larger than `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` by iteratively calling `OptimizedImage.downsize` up to 5 times — but no tests were added or updated for `uploads_controller.rb` or `OptimizedImage.downsize`/`optimize` to verify this logic (e.g., that it stops once the file is small enough, that it gives up after 5 attempts, that it uses the correct dimensions string, or that non-image uploads/API-only cases work as expected). Given the signature changes to `OptimizedImage.downsize`/`optimize` and the new retry loop, this is a risky area to leave untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation crashes with NoMethodError when host is nil

`before_validation { self.host.sub!(...); self.host.sub!(...) }` assumes `host` is always a String. If `host` is nil (e.g. the admin submits the form with no host value, or `params[:embeddable_host][:host]` is missing as set in `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController#save_host`), `self.host.sub!` raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'sub!' for nil:NilClass` instead of surfacing a normal `validates_format_of`/presence validation error. This turns a user input mistake into an unhandled 500 error.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update/destroy do not handle a missing EmbeddableHost record

`EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` returns `nil` when no matching record exists. In `update`, the subsequent `save_host(host)` call will do `host.host = ...` on `nil`, raising `NoMethodError`. In `destroy` (line 15-16), `host.destroy` is called directly on a possibly-nil object, also raising `NoMethodError`. Neither action returns a proper 404/error response for an invalid id; both will surface as unhandled 500 errors instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricator file content doesn't match its filename (content appears swapped)

`spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` now only defines `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)`, while the newly-added `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` defines `Fabricator(:category)`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, and `:private_category`. The contents of the two files appear to have been swapped: the category fabricators ended up in the file named for embeddable hosts, and vice versa. Fabrication doesn't care about filenames so tests still pass, but this is confusing and will mislead future maintainers looking for category or embeddable-host fabricators by filename.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped string interpolation in raw SQL INSERT

`execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)"` interpolates the `host` value (pulled from the old `embeddable_hosts` site setting, which could contain arbitrary characters such as single quotes) directly into the SQL string without using `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.quote` or parameter binding. A host value containing a single quote will break the INSERT (syntax error, migration failure) or corrupt the migration's intent; this is a data-integrity risk in the migration path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when 'embed_category' site_setting was never customized

The migration does `category_id = execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i`. Site settings are normally only persisted in the `site_settings` table when an admin has explicitly changed them from their default value. Since `embed_category` defaulted to `''`, the vast majority of installations will have no row with `name = 'embed_category'`, so the query returns zero rows and `execute(...)[0]` is `nil`. Calling `['id']` on `nil` raises `NoMethodError`, aborting the migration for essentially every typical install (and for test/CI databases that never touched this setting). The fallback for `category_id == 0` is never reached because the exception happens before it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

false_positives.candidate:
New controller spec only checks class inheritance, not actual behavior

Similar to the embeddable_hosts controller spec, this spec for `Admin::EmbeddingController` only checks that it is a subclass of `Admin::AdminController`. The `show`/`update` actions and the `fetch_embedding` before_filter are not tested at all, so regressions in the embedding admin endpoint would not be caught.

New controller spec only checks class inheritance, not actual behavior

The spec for `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` only asserts `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController < Admin::AdminController`. None of the new `create`, `update`, or `destroy` actions (including the error paths discussed above, such as missing-id handling or invalid host validation) are exercised, leaving the new admin endpoints for managing embeddable hosts essentially untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NoMethodError when TopicUser record does not exist

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil (e.g. if the TopicUser row for this user/topic was never created or was deleted), and the following code immediately calls `tu.notification_level` and `tu.notification_level =`, which will raise NoMethodError on nil and return a 500 error instead of gracefully handling the case. There is no `TopicUser.find_or_initialize_by` fallback or nil guard.

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Misspelled method/translation key name 'stopNotificiationsText'

The computed property and its backing translation key use the misspelling 'Notificiations' instead of 'Notifications' (also mirrored in client.en.yml's `stop_notifications` key use and the template). While internally consistent, this typo will persist in the codebase and confuse future maintainers who search for 'notifications'.

false_positives.candidate:
No controller spec added for the new unsubscribe action

The PR adds a new `TopicsController#unsubscribe` action with non-trivial branching logic (slug mismatch redirect, notification level toggling, nil TopicUser handling) but no request/controller spec was added to cover it. Only an unrelated small change to message_builder_spec.rb was made. The new behavior (including the non-idempotent toggle noted above) is untested.

State-mutating action performed via GET request

TopicsController#unsubscribe is only reachable via GET routes (config/routes.rb: `get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"`) yet it mutates `TopicUser#notification_level` and persists it with `tu.save!`. GET requests are expected to be idempotent/safe; browsers/email clients routinely prefetch or re-request GET URLs (link previews, safe-link scanners, page refresh), and because the user must already be logged in (added to `ensure_logged_in`), a logged-in user who simply reloads the unsubscribe page, or who is tricked into navigating to this URL from a third-party page (GET requests are not blocked by SameSite=Lax on top-level navigation), will have their notification level silently changed again. Worse, the toggle logic is not actually idempotent: on the second invocation it moves the state from `regular` to `muted`, progressively down-grading notifications on every reload instead of leaving state unchanged. This should require POST/PUT with explicit CSRF protection, or be made properly idempotent.

Template placed at wrong path for the new top-level 'topicUnsubscribe' route

The route is registered as a top-level, non-nested route: `this.route('topicUnsubscribe', { path: '/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe' });` in app-route-map.js.es6, and its matching controller/view files are dasherized at the top level (`controllers/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6`, `views/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6`). However the template is placed in a nested folder as `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs`, which is the convention used for routes nested under the `topic` resource (e.g. topic.fromParams), not for a standalone dasherized route name. This mismatch is likely to cause the Ember resolver to fail to find the template for the `topicUnsubscribe` route, breaking the newly added feature entirely.

unsubscribe_link changed to multiline block scalar without stripping trailing newline

`unsubscribe_link` was changed from a single-line scalar to a `|` block scalar, which by default preserves a trailing newline. Since `body` appends this string with `body << "\n"; body << I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', ...)`, the resulting plain-text email body will contain extra trailing whitespace/newlines that weren't present before. Using `|-` (strip) would avoid the extra blank line.

unsubscribe_link translation now requires unsubscribe_url, breaking other callers of build_email

The `unsubscribe_link` i18n string (config/locales/server.en.yml) now contains a new interpolation placeholder `%{unsubscribe_url}`. `html_part` and `body` both call `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` whenever `@opts[:add_unsubscribe_link]` is true, without ensuring `unsubscribe_url` is present in `template_args`. Any existing caller of `build_email`/`MessageBuilder` that sets `add_unsubscribe_link: true` but does not also pass `unsubscribe_url` (for example other mailers not touched by this PR, or future/plugin code) will now raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` instead of rendering the email. This is confirmed by the fact that the existing spec in message_builder_spec.rb had to be updated to add `unsubscribe_url` just to keep passing.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? side-effects run multiple times per signup attempt, inflating match_count

`should_block?` is called from the `email` EachValidator, which runs every time `valid?`/`save` triggers validations. In `UsersController#create` (app/controllers/users_controller.rb), `user.valid?` is called once (to decide whether to call DiscourseHub), and then `user.save` triggers validations again internally. This means a single signup attempt against a blocked email can increment `match_count` by 2 (or more, if other code paths call `valid?`), making the recorded match statistics inaccurate and misleading for any analysis or reporting based on `match_count`/`last_match_at`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email matching is case sensitive, allowing trivial bypass

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` using the raw email string passed in from the validator (which in turn comes from `user.email`, which is never normalized/downcased before this check). Since the comparison is a case-sensitive SQL match (and the unique index on `blocked_emails.email` is also case sensitive), an email that was blocked as `bad@spammers.org` can be bypassed simply by registering as `Bad@Spammers.org` or `BAD@SPAMMERS.ORG`. This defeats the entire purpose of the blocked-email feature.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
Account-creation failure response now leaks raw validation errors and submitted email

The `create` action's failure branch now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` to the client. This echoes back the submitted email (even when rejected for being blocked, already taken, or disallowed by whitelist/blacklist) along with the specific validation error keys. This allows an attacker to probe arbitrary email addresses and learn whether they are already registered, blocked, or restricted by domain policy without ever creating an account — a user/email-enumeration vector that did not exist before (previously only a combined message string was exposed).

No test coverage for whitelist/blacklist branches moved out of User model

`app/models/user.rb` previously had `email_validator`/`email_in_restriction_setting?` methods handling `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` and `email_domains_blacklist`, and this logic has been moved into `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`. The new spec file only tests the `BlockedEmail` branch (lines 9-21); it does not exercise the whitelist or blacklist branches (lines 4-12 of email_validator.rb) at all, so a regression in that moved logic (e.g. regex construction, which setting takes precedence) would go undetected. Any prior tests for this logic that existed against `User` should be confirmed as migrated here, otherwise this behavior now has no automated coverage.

Validator always invokes should_block? even with no record errors check limited to one attribute, could run against blank/invalid values

`validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` whenever the whitelist/blacklist checks pass, without guarding against `value` being blank or malformed. Although presence is validated elsewhere on `User`, this validator can be reused on other models/attributes where blank or nil values might reach `should_block?`, causing an unnecessary `BlockedEmail.where(email: nil)` query and wasted BlockedEmail record lookups. A `return if value.blank?` guard would make this validator more robust and reusable.

rejectedEmails array literal shared at prototype definition time

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is defined directly on the controller's prototype as a shared array literal rather than being created fresh per instance (e.g. in an `init` hook). If more than one instance of `CreateAccountController` is ever created (tests, multiple modal opens without a full page reload, etc.), all instances share and mutate the same array, so rejected emails from one session/instance can leak into another, causing emails to be incorrectly reported as previously rejected.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backwards/weak origin check for postMessage listener

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` checks whether `e.origin` is a substring of `discourseUrl`, rather than verifying that `e.origin` strictly equals (or is a prefix of) the Discourse origin. This is the wrong direction for an origin check: a message is accepted as long as `e.origin` happens to appear anywhere inside the `discourseUrl` string, which is a fragile comparison that can behave unexpectedly depending on how `discourseUrl` is configured (e.g. if it contains query params, paths, or other substrings). The check should compare the parsed origin of `discourseUrl` against `e.origin` with strict equality instead of using substring containment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid ERB/Ruby code `end if` breaks template compilation

Line 6 contains `<%- end if %>` which compiles to the Ruby statement `end if` with no preceding expression for the `if` modifier. This is a syntax error and will raise a SyntaxError at template-compile time whenever the `embed/best` view is actually rendered (both when posts are present and when they are not). The controller spec for this action mocks `TopicView.new` and doesn't render views, so this bug is not caught by the included tests. This should simply be `<%- end %>`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError when feed item has no content

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes `i.content` is always present. Many plain RSS 2.0 feeds only populate `<description>`, not `content:encoded`/Atom `<content>`, so `i.content` can be `nil`, raising `NoMethodError: undefined method 'scrub' for nil`. Since `sidekiq_options retry: false` is set on this scheduled job, such an exception will cause polling to silently fail (without retry) for any feed item lacking a content field, and potentially abort processing of all subsequent items in that run since the exception propagates out of the `each` loop.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
Controller spec never renders views, hiding template errors

The success-path examples stub `TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed`/`TopicView.new`/`TopicRetriever` and never actually render `embed/best.html.erb` or `embed/loading.html.erb` (the spec is not configured with `render_views: true`, and `TopicView.new` is merely expected to be called, not exercised). As a result, a real rendering error in the view (such as the invalid `<%- end if %>` in `best.html.erb`) is not caught by this test suite, even though this is the primary new user-facing code path added by the PR.

Disqus import loses category assignment and original post timestamps

The previous implementation created the first post with `category: category_id` (derived from the removed `--category`/`-c` option) and `created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at])`, preserving the thread's original category and creation date during import. The new call `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])` does not accept or forward either a category or a created_at value, so imported Disqus threads are now always created with no category and with the current time as their creation date instead of the original Disqus post date. This is both a feature removal (the `--category` CLI option still exists in `method_option` metadata removed from the diff but no longer has any effect) and a data-fidelity regression for anyone running this migration tool expecting historical dates/categories to be preserved.

Full RSS feed re-poll triggered per unknown embed URL

`perform_retrieve` runs `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})`, which downloads and parses the entire configured feed, every time a never-before-seen `embed_url` is requested and feed polling is enabled — even though the hourly scheduled `PollFeed` job already performs this work independently. The only throttle (`retrieved_recently?`) is keyed per `embed_url`, not per feed, so many distinct unseen embed URLs arriving in a short window (e.g. several different articles being embedded concurrently) can each trigger a full, redundant feed fetch/parse, which is wasteful and could amplify load against the external feed host.

Unguarded race condition on `embed_url` uniqueness in TopicEmbed.import

`self.import` does a plain `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` check and, if blank, proceeds to create a new Topic/Post and then `TopicEmbed.create!` inside a `Topic.transaction` block. There is no locking (e.g. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) around the blank-check, so two concurrent callers for the same `embed_url` (e.g. the hourly `PollFeed` job and a simultaneous `TopicRetriever`-triggered import from a visitor request) can both see `embed.blank? == true` and both attempt to create a topic/post and a `TopicEmbed` row. The unique index on `embed_url` (added in the accompanying migration) will cause the second `TopicEmbed.create!` to raise `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique`, which is not rescued here, potentially leaving an orphaned Topic/Post with no corresponding `TopicEmbed` record if the surrounding nested transaction semantics don't fully roll back the already-created post (PostCreator#create uses its own internal `Post.transaction`).

cook_method :raw_html bypasses sanitization entirely for imported content

`cook` returns `raw` unmodified when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, skipping the normal PrettyText rendering/sanitization pipeline. `TopicEmbed.import` (used both by `PollFeed` and by `TopicRetriever`/`import_remote`) creates posts with this cook_method, and the resulting `cooked` value is rendered unescaped via `<%= raw post.cooked %>` in `embed/best.html.erb` as well as in the normal topic view used throughout the rest of the application. Content coming from `PollFeed` (`TopicEmbed.import(user, url, i.title, content)`) is taken directly from the RSS/Atom feed with no tag allow-list (unlike `import_remote`, which at least constrains tags via Readability's `tags:`/`attributes:` options). A malicious or compromised feed can therefore inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that is stored verbatim and rendered without sanitization to every visitor of the topic, constituting a stored XSS vector.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

false_positives.candidate:
Float-based child layout left in place after converting `.small-action` to flexbox

`.small-action` was converted to `display: flex` (lines 264-265), but its children `.topic-avatar` (line 270, `float: left`) and `button` (line 309, `float: right`) still rely on `float` for positioning. The CSS flexbox spec explicitly makes `float` a no-op on flex items, so these floats no longer have any effect. As a result the avatar is no longer guaranteed to sit to the left and the trailing button is no longer pushed to the right — the three children (`.topic-avatar`, `.small-action-desc`, `button`) will instead lay out in normal flex row order with no explicit `order`/`margin-left:auto` compensation, which changes the visual layout from what was previously intended.

Removed `.badge-wrapper.bullet { margin-top: 5px; }` without a compensating rule

The previous nested rule setting `margin-top: 5px` on `.badge-wrapper.bullet` inside `.extra-info-wrapper` was deleted with no replacement. This was presumably used to vertically align the bullet badge within the line; removing it without adding any corresponding alignment (e.g. via flex `align-items`) risks a vertical misalignment regression for bullet-style category badges in the extra-info area.

Removed `padding-top: 4px` from `.small-action-desc > p` without explanation

The `padding-top: 4px` previously applied to the first-level paragraph inside `.small-action-desc` was removed. Combined with the other spacing changes in this same selector block, this reduces vertical spacing that may have been needed for readability/alignment of the small-action description text, and there is no indication this was deliberate given the PR description does not explain the rationale.

`.small-action-desc` left padding drastically reduced, likely causing overlap with the icon

`padding: 0.5em 0 0.5em 4em;` was changed to `padding: 0 1.5%;`. The original 4em left padding was almost certainly reserved to make room for the floated `.topic-avatar` icon (45px wide, set via `.topic-avatar i { width: 45px; }`). false_positives.candidate:
Default member page size silently reduced for automatic groups

The previous implementation gave automatic groups a larger default limit (200) specifically to work around truncation for groups with many members, while non-automatic groups were unpaginated/unlimited. The new code applies a flat default `limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` to all groups regardless of the `automatic` flag. This is a behavior change for the public `/groups/:group_id/members` endpoint: large automatic groups (e.g. trust-level groups) that used to return up to 200 members by default now only return 50, which can break any existing API consumers or UI relying on the previous default page size, without any changelog/doc update reflecting this change.

Membership mutation is persisted before validation/save, causing misleading error responses

In `remove_member`, `group.users.delete(user_id)` (line 90) immediately executes a DELETE against the join table for a persisted `group`/association, and in `add_members`, `group.add(user)` (line 73) similarly persists membership immediately via the association. Only afterwards is `group.save` called to determine the HTTP response. If `group.save` fails for any unrelated reason (e.g. stale validation state), the controller renders `render_json_error(group)` even though the membership change has already been committed to the database. Clients receiving an error response will believe the operation failed and may retry, potentially causing duplicate adds or confusing inconsistent state, since the actual membership mutation already succeeded independent of the `save` result.

`admin.groups.selector_placeholder` was changed from "add users" to "enter username" (singular). However, the `user-selector` field it labels (used in `admin/templates/group.hbs`) accepts a comma-separated list of usernames that are split and processed as multiple users in `addMembers`/`Admin::GroupsController#add_members`. The new singular wording suggests only one username can be entered, which is misleading to admins trying to add multiple members at once.

`remove_member` calls `group.users.delete(user_id)` with a raw integer id and no rescue. Depending on how the has_many association's `delete` resolves an id that is not currently part of the group's collection (e.g. stale client state, concurrent removal, or a malicious/incorrect user_id), this can raise `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound`, which is not rescued here and would bubble up as an unhandled 500 error instead of a clean validation error response. There is also no spec covering this scenario (see spec/controllers/admin/groups_controller_spec.rb), so this regression path is untested.

The `addMembers` action contains a `// TODO: should clear the input` comment acknowledging that `this.get("usernames")` is never reset after a successful add. This means the previously entered usernames remain in the input field after the members are added, and clicking "Add" again (or forgetting the field still has old content) will re-submit the same usernames, causing redundant/no-op requests and a confusing UX for admins managing group membership.

`automatic` lookup in item view template resolves against the member, not the group

`group_member.hbs` is rendered as the template for the `group-member` itemView used via `{{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}` in `group.hbs`. Since this is the non-block `{{each}}` form with an `itemView`, the rendering context for each item's template is the member object itself, not the outer group/controller context. The bare `{{#unless automatic}}` check in this template therefore resolves `automatic` against the `member` (a user object, which has no `automatic` property) rather than against the group's `automatic` flag, so it will always be falsy and the remove link will be rendered for members of automatic groups too, even though removal is disallowed server-side. The `addMembers` action (line 61-65) calls `this.get("model").addMembers(this.get("usernames"))` and `removeMember` (line 51-59) calls `self.get("model").removeMember(member)` without attaching a `.catch`/error handler on the returned promise, unlike `save` and `destroy` which do handle rejection with `bootbox.alert`. The backend (`Admin::GroupsController#add_members`/`#remove_member`) returns a 422 with an error message when the group is automatic, or can fail for other reasons (e.g. unknown usernames silently skipped, group save validation failure). Because there is no error handler, any such failure is silently swallowed in the UI and the user gets no feedback that the add/remove operation did not succeed.

false_positives.candidate:
Custom FallbackLocaleList replaces full-featured I18n::Locale::Fallbacks with a minimal stand-in

Previously `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` assigned a standard `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` instance, which implements the full fallback API (`map`, `default`, `defaults`, locale-tag decomposition such as `pt-BR -> pt -> en`, etc.). The new `FallbackLocaleList` only overrides `[]` and `ensure_loaded!`; all other Hash/Fallbacks methods are either absent or behave as an empty Hash. Any code (core, plugin, or gem) that calls other methods on `I18n.fallbacks` besides `[]` will now silently misbehave or raise NoMethodError, and locale-tag-based fallback behavior (e.g. regional variants) is lost without an equivalent compatibility shim.

Fallback behavior is now enabled globally instead of per-environment, silently changing dev/test behavior

`config.i18n.fallbacks = true` was previously set only in production.rb, profile.rb and the cloud66 production.rb — i.e. selectively per environment. By moving the equivalent logic into `config/initializers/i18n.rb` (which loads for all environments including development and test), locale fallbacks are now always active everywhere. This is a behavior change that isn't called out in the PR description, and it means missing-translation issues that previously surfaced in development/test (because fallback wasn't enabled there) will now be silently masked by falling back to the default locale/English, potentially hiding real translation bugs until they reach users of other locales in production.

No tests added for the new fallback resolution logic

The PR introduces new runtime logic (`FallbackLocaleList#[]`, `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!`, `I18n.ensure_loaded!` in translate_accelerator.rb, and the new call in `ApplicationController#set_locale`) but adds no specs verifying that: (1) translations correctly fall back from user locale -> site default locale -> English, (2) `ensure_loaded!` actually loads the right locale files, or (3) `set_locale` behaves correctly when a translation is missing in the user's locale. Given this is a user-facing localization feature, lacking any automated coverage is a significant gap.

PR description is a non-descriptive placeholder

The PR description is simply "Test 9", which provides no information about the rationale, scope, or testing performed for this localization fallback feature. This makes it difficult for reviewers or future maintainers to understand why the change was made or what edge cases were considered.

Required initializer ordering is enforced only by a comment, not by code

The file relies on `02-freedom_patches.rb` having already patched `I18n::Backend::Simple`/`I18n::Backend::Base` (translate_accelerator) before this initializer runs, but the only indication of that dependency is the comment `# order: after 02-freedom_patches.rb`. Rails initializer load order is driven by filename sort order; there is no explicit `require` or `config.before_initialize`/`after_initialize` hook enforcing the sequence. If the freedom-patch filename or load mechanism changes, this file could load before the patches are applied, causing `I18n::Backend::Simple` to not have the LRU-cache/explicit-load behavior when `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` is mixed in, or vice versa, leading to subtle load-order bugs.

ensure_loaded! recomputes fallback chain (including a SiteSetting lookup) on every request

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is invoked unconditionally in `set_locale`, a before_filter run on every request. Internally this calls `FallbackLocaleList#[]`, which reads `SiteSetting.default_locale` on every single request just to build the (mostly already-loaded) fallback chain. While the actual file loading is memoized via `@loaded_locales`, the SiteSetting lookup and array construction happen on every request regardless, adding avoidable per-request overhead that the translate_accelerator patch was specifically designed to minimize.

Previously (in Python, `_load_segment_data`), when a segment exceeded `max_segment_spans`, the whole segment was dropped and a metric (`spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded`) plus an error log were emitted, making this clearly observable. Now the eviction happens inside the Lua script via `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`, silently discarding the oldest-scored (earliest end_timestamp) spans whenever a segment exceeds 1000 entries, with no corresponding metric or log anywhere in the codebase. This is a data-integrity/observability regression: oversized segments are now silently truncated instead of being flagged, and operators have no way to detect how often or how severely this occurs.

Unrelated, under-reviewed feature bundled into a PR about span-buffer eviction

This PR's title/description describe an optimization to span buffer insertion/eviction, yet the bulk of the diff (OptimizedCursorPaginator, the new `optimized_pagination` endpoint branch, and the Cursor negative-offset comment) is an unrelated pagination feature exposed to privileged users with dubious safety claims ('This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level') that does not actually prevent the negative-offset crash described in another finding. Bundling a large, untested, security-adjacent feature into a PR ostensibly about Redis Lua script changes makes this hard to review properly and should be split out or justified separately.

The `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter (default 1001) is no longer referenced anywhere in buffer.py after this change — the span-count limiting logic that previously used it in `_load_segment_data` (checking `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`) has been removed and replaced by a hardcoded cutoff of 1000 inside `add-buffer.lua` (`zpopmin` when `span_count > 1000`). Any caller setting a custom `max_segment_spans` value now has zero effect, and the hardcoded Lua threshold (1000) is inconsistent with the old default (1001), making the parameter dead and misleading.

The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only rewrites a column when, after lowering and stripping, it equals exactly `"count()"`. Any variant such as an already-aliased column (`"count() as total"`), an equation wrapping count (`"equation|count() / 2"`), or extra internal whitespace (`"count( )"`) will not match and will silently fall through unmodified, meaning the upsampling transform silently fails to apply for these forms while the caller believes upsampling is enabled. This can produce inconsistent results between different query shapes (e.g., top-events queries that generate aliased column strings) without any error or log indicating the transform was skipped.

The test file exercises the private helpers `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, and `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`, but never tests the actual public function `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, which contains the new caching logic (cache hit/miss paths, TTL, and the AND-combination with `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`). `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is also completely untested. Since the caching behavior is the core 'performance optimization' being introduced by this PR, and is the most likely place for subtle bugs (e.g., stale cache across allowlist changes), this is a significant gap in test coverage.

Substring match for error-focused query misclassifies negated queries

`_is_error_focused_query` determines whether a discover query is error-focused by checking if the literal substring "event.type:error" appears anywhere in the lowercased query string. This naive check does not account for negation: a query like `!event.type:error` (which explicitly excludes error events) contains the substring "event.type:error" and will be incorrectly classified as error-focused. As a result, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` will return True and `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` will rewrite `count()` into `upsampled_count() as count` (a `sum(sample_weight)` aggregation) for a query that is explicitly NOT about errors, producing wrong/garbage counts (or query errors if `sample_weight` is absent for non-error rows) for any caller using negated error filters.

This PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing a git submodule-style reference ("Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a") pointing back to the base commit of this very repository. This is unrelated to the error-upsampling feature described in the PR and looks like an accidental artifact (e.g., a nested git clone or submodule added by mistake). It should be removed before merge since it can confuse git tooling, bloat the repository, or break CI checkout steps that don't expect a submodule here.

The only real mitigation against a stale allowlist decision is the 60-second TTL in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`. The new `upsampled_count` SnQL function computes `toInt64(sum(Column("sample_weight")))` and is used as a drop-in replacement for `count()` whenever upsampling is enabled for a project. The code comments explicitly assume 'the database schema ensures sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects' without any validation or test covering historical/non-sampled events, making this a real data-correctness risk if that assumption doesn't hold.

Backup codes stored with reversible symmetric encryption instead of one-way hashing

Backup codes are generated in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts and stored via symmetricEncrypt (reversible) using CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY, the same key used for the TOTP secret. Unlike passwords, which are hashed one-way, backup codes act as long-lived authentication secrets (similar to passwords) and should be hashed (e.g. bcrypt/argon2) rather than symmetrically encrypted. If the encryption key and database are both compromised, all users' backup codes can be recovered in plaintext, allowing full account takeover bypassing 2FA. This is a weaker security posture than expected for a credential of this type.

If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (Escape key, clicking the overlay, navigating away and back, etc. via the Dialog's onOpenChange), onEnable() is never called and resetState() never runs, so the parent's UI (e.g. the two-factor switch) can remain stale/unchecked even though 2FA is actually enabled server-side. `if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw ...` is unreliable: `statusText` is not guaranteed to be the literal string "OK" across all environments/HTTP versions (e.g., HTTP/2 responses commonly have an empty statusText), and conversely a non-200 response could still have statusText "OK" in rare cases. This should check `response.ok` or `response.status === 200` instead, otherwise valid refresh responses can be incorrectly treated as failures (or vice versa).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

false_positives.candidate:
CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME is not normalized to lowercase

`.env.example` documents that `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` 'should be in lowercase', but the code never lowercases the configured value before using it as a key into `req.headers`. Node/Next.js always lowercases incoming header names, so if an operator sets this env var with any uppercase character, the lookup will always miss and the webhook will always return 403, with no indication of why. The code should normalize the header name itself (e.g. `.toLowerCase()`) instead of relying on operator discipline.

No automated tests for new credential-sync logic

The PR adds several new, trust-sensitive pieces of logic (the `/api/webhook/app-credential` endpoint, `refreshOAuthTokens`, and `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) that directly affect how OAuth credentials are persisted, but no unit or integration tests were added for any of them (the author's own checklist states tests were not added). Given the data-corruption risks identified in the token-refresh code paths, this is an area that should have had test coverage before merging.

Non constant-time secret comparison and no HTTP method restriction

The webhook secret check (`req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`) uses a plain string inequality comparison, which is vulnerable to timing attacks that could help an attacker brute-force the secret. Additionally, the handler never checks `req.method`, so it will process the body on any HTTP verb that reaches it (not just POST), and malformed/invalid encrypted payloads (`symmetricDecrypt` / `JSON.parse` failures) are not caught, resulting in an unhandled exception and a generic 500 instead of a controlled error response.

Salesforce access token is unconditionally refreshed on every CalendarService instantiation

Unlike every other provider in this PR, `getClient` performs an OAuth refresh-token request unconditionally, with no check of whether the current access token is still valid (there is no `isTokenValid`/expiry check before calling the Salesforce token endpoint). Since `getClient` runs in the constructor and a new `SalesforceCalendarService` is created per operation, this triggers an extra network round-trip and a token refresh call to Salesforce on every single booking/calendar action, which is wasteful and can hit Salesforce's rate limits. It also introduces a concurrency risk: concurrent requests using the same credential will each attempt to refresh the token independently, risking invalidation/race conditions if Salesforce invalidates the previous access token on refresh.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Incorrect boolean logic makes team-admin/owner permission check nearly always false

The permission check uses `&&` instead of `||`:
```
const isTeamAdminOrOwner =
    (await isTeamAdmin(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0)) &&
    (await isTeamOwner(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0));
```
Since a membership typically has exactly one role (MEMBER, ADMIN, or OWNER), a user can almost never satisfy both `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner` simultaneously. This means the variable named `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is effectively always `false`, so team admins and owners who are not themselves the booking organizer or an attendee will be rejected with FORBIDDEN when trying to add guests, defeating the intent of granting admins/owners this permission.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Guest emails deduped against existing attendees but not against each other, and comparison is case-sensitive

`uniqueGuests` is filtered only against `booking.attendees` (`!booking.attendees.some(...)`) and does not remove duplicate entries within the submitted `guests` array itself, nor normalize case. If duplicates (or case-variant duplicates, e.g. `a@b.com` vs `A@B.com`) are submitted in a single call -- which bypasses the client-side `AddGuestsDialog` uniqueness check if called directly via API -- multiple attendee rows with effectively the same email can be created via `createMany`, leading to duplicate attendee records on the booking.

false_positives.candidate:
No automated tests for the new addGuests feature

This PR introduces a brand-new mutation (`addGuestsHandler`), a new dialog (`AddGuestsDialog`), and a new reusable form component (`MultiEmail`), none of which have accompanying unit or integration tests. Given the handler contains non-trivial permission logic (which is already buggy, see other findings) and mutates booking/attendee data plus triggers calendar updates and emails, the lack of tests is a significant gap for verifying correct behavior and preventing regressions.

No check that booking is not cancelled before adding guests

The handler fetches the booking and performs permission checks but never verifies the booking's status (e.g. `CANCELLED`/`REJECTED`). This allows adding guests to cancelled or rejected bookings, which doesn't make logical sense and could trigger calendar/video updates and emails for events that no longer exist.

No upper bound on number of guests that can be added in a single request

`guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no maximum length constraint. A caller could submit an arbitrarily large array of guest emails in one request, causing a large number of attendee rows to be created and a large number of emails to be queued/sent in one `addGuestsHandler` invocation, which is a potential performance/abuse concern for a mutation exposed to any authenticated attendee/organizer.

Team members never notified because evt.team is never populated

`sendAddGuestsEmails` in email-manager.ts iterates `calendarEvent.team?.members` to notify all team members with `OrganizerAddGuestsEmail`, but the `CalendarEvent` object (`evt`) constructed in `addGuestsHandler` never sets a `team` property. As a result, `calendarEvent.team` is always `undefined` for this flow, so the team-member notification loop is dead code and only the single organizer email (from `booking.userId`) ever receives the organizer notification for team-based bookings, even though other team members may need to be informed guests were added.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteMany retryCount condition is not scoped to SMS method

The second branch of the OR clause in the deleteMany call (`retryCount: { gt: 1 }`) has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` restriction, unlike the first branch. Since `retryCount` is a generic field on the shared `WorkflowReminder` model (also used, e.g., by `WebhookScheduledTriggers`-like retry concepts, or potentially by future email/WhatsApp retry logic), any WorkflowReminder row of any method that ends up with retryCount > 1 will be permanently deleted by this SMS-specific cron endpoint, even if it is an EMAIL or WHATSAPP reminder unrelated to SMS sending. This can cause unintended data loss for non-SMS reminders if retryCount is ever incremented elsewhere, and is inconsistent with the stated intent of only cleaning up failed SMS reminders.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

false_positives.candidate:
Catch block treats all errors as SMS send failures, risking premature deletion

The try block spans many operations beyond the actual SMS send: fetching the organizer's profile, resolving the booker URL, parsing booking metadata, rendering templates, etc. Any exception from these unrelated operations (e.g., a transient DB query failure, a template rendering bug, or a metadata parsing error) is caught by the same catch block and increments `retryCount` exactly like a genuine SMS delivery failure (e.g., invalid phone number). Combined with the new deletion logic (retryCount > 1 triggers deletion), two unrelated/transient errors on a reminder are enough to have it permanently deleted, even though the actual SMS send may never have been attempted or may have been perfectly deliverable. This conflates infrastructure/transient errors with the specific 'invalid phone number'-type failures the PR intends to handle, risking silent loss of valid reminders.

Missing test coverage for new retryCount/deletion behavior

This PR introduces non-trivial new behavior (incrementing retryCount on failure, and deleting reminders once retryCount exceeds 1) but no tests were added or updated to verify: (1) retryCount increments correctly on both the 'no scheduledSMS result' path and the exception path, (2) the deleteMany call actually removes reminders with retryCount > 1, and (3) it does not inadvertently remove unrelated reminders. Given this logic directly affects whether customer-facing SMS reminders get silently dropped, the lack of test coverage is a notable gap for a bug-fix PR.

No retry/cleanup path when message or sendTo is empty

When `message` is falsy/empty or `sendTo` is missing, the code silently does nothing (no retryCount increment, no scheduling, no logging). Such reminders remain `scheduled: false` indefinitely and are only ever cleaned up once their `scheduledDate` passes (via the first deleteMany branch), meaning they can linger unprocessed for up to 7 days without any retryCount-based accounting or visibility, unlike the newly added failure paths. This inconsistency was not addressed by this PR despite being a closely related failure mode (e.g., a booking never had a phone number set).

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Array-based ANY(...) SQL conditions for team/org scope are never executed against the real database in tests

`buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` and `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` build SQL like `("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})) AND (...)` where `teamIds`/`userIdsFromTeam` are JS number arrays interpolated via Prisma.sql. Passing arrays as parameters to `ANY()` in raw Postgres queries can require explicit type casts (e.g. `ANY($1::int[])`) depending on the driver/parameter binding, otherwise Postgres may fail with a parameter type inference error at execution time. The only integration test that actually executes a query via `prisma.$queryRaw` (the renamed `getBaseConditions` test) exercises the 'user' scope, which does not use `ANY()`. The 'team' and 'org' scope tests only assert structural equality of the constructed `Prisma.Sql` object and never actually run the query against the database, so a runtime failure in the ANY()-array binding for team/org scopes (explicitly called out as a risk in the PR's own review checklist) would not be caught by these tests.

Caching behavior tests were removed even though the caching logic still exists in the service

The previous test suite had a `describe("Caching", ...)` block verifying that `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()` return cached results on subsequent calls (backed by `cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions` fields). This PR deletes those tests entirely without replacing them, while the service implementation (`insightsBooking.ts`) still contains and relies on this same caching mechanism (fields `cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions`, lines 49-50 and 83-95). Removing these tests silently drops coverage for an existing, still-present feature, so a regression in caching (e.g., accidentally rebuilding the Prisma.Sql object on each call, or caching stale/incorrect conditions) would go undetected.

PR description scope does not match actual diff contents

The PR description states this change only updates the integration test file to match a service implementation that was 'previously converted' to Prisma.sql, implying `insightsBooking.ts` itself was not modified by this PR. However the diff shows substantial changes to `insightsBooking.ts` (import change from `import type { Prisma }` to `import { Prisma }`, removal of `findMany`, new `getBaseConditions` method, rewritten condition-building logic). This mismatch between the stated scope and the actual change makes it harder for reviewers to know which parts of the service logic are newly introduced in this PR versus pre-existing, and increases risk that the 'HIGH RISK' authorization/SQL logic in the service itself did not receive a dedicated, scoped review.

Public findMany() method removed and replaced with getBaseConditions(), breaking the service's contract

The previous implementation exposed `findMany(findManyArgs)` which executed the query against `bookingTimeStatusDenormalized` and returned rows. This PR removes that method entirely and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns a `Prisma.Sql` fragment and requires the caller to manually construct and execute a raw `$queryRaw` query (as the test now does). Any production code that calls `InsightsBookingService.findMany(...)` (e.g. insights routes/UI data fetchers) will fail to compile/run after this change, since the method no longer exists. The PR description claims this is only a test update to match an already-converted implementation, but the diff shows the public API of the service itself is being changed in the same PR, which is a contract break that isn't validated against other call sites in the diff.

Cache deletion bypasses CalendarCacheRepository abstraction

No tests added for the destructive deleteCache feature

This PR introduces a new destructive mutation (`deleteCacheHandler`), a new UI component (`CredentialActionsDropdown`) with confirmation dialogs, and a new repository method (`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`), but no unit or integration tests were added for any of them. Given that deleteCache permanently removes cached calendar availability data and the PR's own review checklist flags end-to-end verification as still outstanding, lack of automated test coverage for authorization (credential ownership check) and the delete logic itself is a notable gap.

deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars query

dev:cron now relies on npx tsx without adding tsx as a dependency

The `dev:cron` script was changed from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but `tsx` is not added to `devDependencies` (only `ts-node` remains, still used by other scripts). updateManyByCredentialId updates all SelectedCalendars, not just the ones refreshed

`fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` calls `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` after processing only the `selectedCalendars` passed into the function. However `updateManyByCredentialId` updates every SelectedCalendar row for that credentialId, including rows that were not part of the batch being refreshed (e.g. in `unwatchCalendar`, `remainingCalendars` excludes the calendar being unwatched, yet its `updatedAt` would still be bumped by this call). For call sites where the parent record isn't deleted via cascade afterwards (e.g. handleNewBooking.ts's reschedule flow, which does not delete the original booking or its reminders), this leaves a permanently 'scheduled: true' WorkflowReminder row in the database that is never updated. It will only eventually get swept up by scheduleEmailReminders.ts's blanket 'scheduledDate <= now' deleteMany once its date has passed, meaning stale/incorrect reminder records persist for potentially days.

false_positives.candidate:
A single failed cancellation aborts the whole cancellation batch, leaving earlier successes undeleted

The entire cancel loop (SendGrid request + collecting delete promises) is wrapped in one try/catch, and the collected `workflowRemindersToDelete` are only awaited after the for-loop completes. If the SendGrid cancel request throws for any single reminder mid-loop, the exception propagates out of the loop before `Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)` is reached, so none of the already-successfully-cancelled reminders processed earlier in the same run get their DB rows deleted. This causes redundant repeat cancellation calls on the next CRON run and delays cleanup, and masks partial failures since only one generic console.log is emitted for the whole batch.

No automated tests cover the new deferred-cancellation CRON logic

This PR introduces the core fix (the `cancelled` flag on WorkflowReminder plus new logic in scheduleEmailReminders.ts to batch-cancel reminders within the next hour), but no tests were added to verify that reminders marked cancelled are correctly filtered by method/date, that the SendGrid cancel call is made with the right batch id, or that DB rows are cleaned up appropriately. Given the bug this PR fixes was itself a silent failure mode (reminders sent despite being 'cancelled'), lack of test coverage for this exact mechanism increases the risk of a future regression going unnoticed.

Reschedule flow still immediately cancels SendGrid-scheduled email reminders, reintroducing the exact bug this PR fixes

In the reschedule branch, deleteScheduledEmailReminder is called with immediateDelete=true (`deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)`), which calls the SendGrid '/v3/user/scheduled_sends' cancel endpoint synchronously instead of deferring to the new `cancelled` flag + CRON mechanism. The whole point of this PR is that immediate SendGrid cancellation can fail once the account hits the 100-pending-cancellations limit, silently letting the old reminder email go out. By keeping immediateDelete=true specifically for rescheduled bookings (the scenario explicitly named in the PR title), this path is not actually fixed: under load, rescheduled-booking reminder emails can still be sent even though they were supposed to be cancelled. Other call sites (handleCancelBooking.ts, bookings.tsx requestReschedule) correctly omit the third argument so cancellation is deferred.

Workflow deletion still cancels all scheduled email reminders immediately instead of deferring

In the `delete` mutation, scheduled EMAIL reminders are cancelled with `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` (immediateDelete=true), issuing an immediate SendGrid cancel call for every reminder instead of using the new deferred `cancelled` flag mechanism this PR introduces to avoid the SendGrid pending-cancellations limit. For a popular workflow with many active bookings and scheduled reminders, deleting it could still trigger the same 100-pending-cancellation failure mode described in the PR, silently letting some reminder emails go out despite the workflow being deleted.

remindersToCancel query lacks a method filter, risking SendGrid API misuse on non-email reminders

The `remindersToCancel` query filters only by `cancelled: true` and `scheduledDate`, without restricting `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` (unlike the deleteMany cleanup query above it and the unscheduledReminders query below it, both of which filter by method). The subsequent loop unconditionally sends every matched reminder's `referenceId` to the SendGrid `/v3/user/scheduled_sends` cancel endpoint as a `batch_id`. If an SMS WorkflowReminder is ever marked `cancelled: true` (currently not done by the SMS manager, but nothing in the schema or type system prevents it), its Twilio SID would be sent to SendGrid, which would fail or behave unpredictably, and the record would still be deleted from the DB as if it had been properly cancelled via Twilio.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are triggered eagerly, defeating the purpose of async/lazy loading

Every property in the appStore object literal calls `import("./appName")` directly as part of module evaluation. Because these import() calls are not wrapped in a function/getter, they execute as soon as `packages/app-store/index.ts` is first required, i.e. all 29 app packages begin loading immediately, exactly like the previous eager `import * as` style, just now wrapped in Promises. To actually get on-demand loading, each entry would need to be a function (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) invoked only when a specific app key is accessed.

This PR changes the fundamental contract of `appStore` from a synchronous object of modules to an object of Promises, requiring every consumer to `await appStore[key]` (and `getCalendar`, `getVideoAdapters`, etc. to become async). Several call sites across the codebase needed manual fixes in this very PR (some still incomplete, e.g. forEach(async...) patterns). No tests were added to verify that all current and future consumers correctly await these values, leaving the change prone to silent regressions where a missed `await` returns a Promise where a `Calendar`/`VideoApiAdapter` instance was expected.

Recurring-event calendar deletion still uses unfixed forEach(async ...), unlike the sibling block fixed a few lines below

Same forEach(async ...) try/catch defect as vital/lib/reschedule.ts

forEach(async ...) with no awaiting or error handling for calendar/video cleanup during reschedule

`dateOverrides.find(...)` stops at the first override entry whose date matches the slot's date and makes the availability decision based solely on that entry, setting `dateOverrideExist = true` as a side effect inside the callback. If a schedule has multiple override time ranges for the same date (which Cal.com's UI allows, e.g. split availability on one date), only the first range in array order is evaluated; subsequent ranges for that date are silently ignored, which can incorrectly mark a slot as unavailable (or available) when a later override entry for the same date would have produced a different result.

Duplicated, divergently-implemented date-override timezone logic

Date-override timezone adjustment is now implemented twice with different math: once here (DST-diff based, using `dayjs().tz(...).utcOffset() - startOfInviteeDay.tz(...).utcOffset()`), and separately in packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts's checkIfIsAvailable (plain `utcOffset()` diff with no DST adjustment). Because both paths independently decide whether an override applies/at what time, and they can diverge (e.g., around DST transitions), the two filters can disagree on the same slot, making the overall availability result inconsistent and harder to reason about or fix in only one place.

No test coverage for the headline round-robin fixed-host date-override fix

The PR description states its main purpose is fixing that fixed-host date overrides are respected for round-robin events (Fixes #8207), with explicit manual test steps involving a round-robin event with a fixed host and a round-robin host. However, the only test added in this file extends the existing single-user 'Check for Date overrides' test with a different invitee timezone; there is no new test exercising a ROUND_ROBIN event type with a fixed host plus override, nor verifying that round-robin host overrides don't block availability while fixed-host overrides do. This leaves the primary bug fix unverified by automated tests.

Timezone offset calculation depends on server's local timezone via Date.toString()

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` and the analogous invitee line convert the Date to a string via `Date.prototype.toString()` before re-parsing with dayjs. `toString()` renders the date using the host process's system timezone, so the resulting calendar date fed into `.tz()` can shift depending on where the Node process runs (and can roll over to an adjacent day near local midnight). This makes the organizer/invitee UTC-offset difference used for date-override conversion non-deterministic across deployment environments, instead of being based purely on the override's actual UTC instant.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard likely never true for spawn-context processes, so .kill() is silently skipped

_ensure_processes_alive() now only calls process.kill() when isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is true. Processes here are created via self.mp_context.Process where self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context('spawn'); such a call returns an instance of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which is a sibling of (not a subclass of) the generic multiprocessing.context.Process class that multiprocessing.Process refers to. Consequently this isinstance check evaluates to False for real spawned subprocesses, meaning the unhealthy process is never killed before _create_process_for_shards spawns its replacement. Previously .kill() was called unconditionally (only ValueError was swallowed), so this is a regression: hung/unhealthy processes may now keep running alongside their replacements, consuming Redis connections and potentially double-producing flushed segments to Kafka.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() aborts terminating remaining flusher processes once the deadline is hit for one process

In join(), the for-loop over self.processes.items() does `break` when the join deadline has passed for the *current* process index. Because break exits the entire for-loop (not just the inner while), any processes that come later in the dict are never waited on nor have .terminate() called on them. Previously there was only a single process and .terminate() was always reached after the wait loop; now, with multiple flusher processes, a timed-out shutdown can leave one or more real subprocesses running un-terminated after join() returns, leaking Kafka producer connections and Redis clients/orphaned processes.

By default this still runs as a single flusher process handling all shards, identical to pre-PR behavior, unless operators explicitly raise --flusher-processes. Memory usage may be double-counted across per-process shard buffers when computing backpressure threshold

submit() now sums buffer.get_memory_info() across self.buffers.values(), where each buffer is a SpansBuffer scoped only to the shards owned by one flusher process. Previously a single SpansBuffer covering all assigned shards computed memory info once per distinct Redis node/cluster. If multiple shards (now split across different per-process buffers) map to the same underlying Redis node, that node's ServiceMemory will be reported and summed multiple times, inflating 'used'/'available' totals used to decide spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage backpressure. This can skew the used/available ratio and trigger (or fail to trigger) hard backpressure incorrectly depending on how shards are distributed across nodes and processes.

test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts len(flusher.processes), max_processes, num_processes and the total shard count in process_to_shards_map; it never submits spans, advances the clock, and verifies that segments for shards handled by different processes are actually flushed/produced correctly, nor does it exercise the per-process restart path added in this PR.
