false_positives.candidate:
Misleading docstring claiming backpressure that doesn't exist

The docstring of `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` (and similarly `FixedQueuePool`) states 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' as a guaranteed property, but the underlying `queue.Queue` objects are created with no `maxsize`, so they never 'fill up' and no backpressure is ever applied to the Kafka consumer. This documentation is inaccurate and could mislead future maintainers into believing memory/backlog growth is bounded when it is not.

No test coverage for partition revocation/reassignment (rebalance)

None of the new tests in test_queue_consumer.py or the thread-queue-parallel tests added to tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py exercise calling `create_with_partitions` more than once on the same `ResultsStrategyFactory`/`queue_pool`, or calling `close()`/`terminate()` on the returned `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` followed by a second `create_with_partitions` call (which is what happens on a real Kafka consumer group rebalance). This leaves the critical bug where `strategy.close()` kills the shared `FixedQueuePool` permanently (see queue_consumer.py close()/terminate()) completely uncovered by tests, even though rebalances are a normal and frequent occurrence in production Kafka consumers.

Shared FixedQueuePool is permanently destroyed by per-rebalance strategy close()/terminate()

ResultsStrategyFactory creates a single `FixedQueuePool` instance once in `__init__` (result_consumer.py, inside `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)`), intended to live for the lifetime of the consumer process and be reused across partition rebalances. However, `create_with_partitions` builds a brand-new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` every time it is called (e.g. on every rebalance), and that strategy's `close()`/`terminate()` methods (queue_consumer.py lines 335-342) call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets every worker thread's `shutdown` flag and shuts down every underlying `queue.Queue`. Arroyo calls `close()`/`terminate()` on the active strategy whenever partitions are revoked (which happens on every consumer group rebalance), and then calls `create_with_partitions` again for the new assignment. Because the factory still holds the same (now permanently dead) `queue_pool` object, the new strategy submits work items into queues whose worker threads have already exited, so no further messages are ever processed after the first rebalance - the consumer silently stalls without raising any error, with no new offsets being committed from that point forward.

Unsynchronized dict mutation/iteration race in OffsetTracker

`OffsetTracker` protects each partition's offset *set* with a per-partition lock, but the outer dictionaries (`all_offsets`, `outstanding`, `last_committed`, `partition_locks`) have no lock guarding structural changes. `get_committable_offsets()` does `for partition in list(self.all_offsets.keys())` (line 74) while `add_offset()` (called from the consumer thread) can concurrently insert a brand-new partition key into the same defaultdict via `self.all_offsets[partition]`. Mutating a dict's size while another thread is iterating/snapshotting its keys can intermittently raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` in CPython, since `add_offset` and `get_committable_offsets`/`mark_committed` run on different threads (main consumer thread vs. the dedicated commit thread) without a shared lock around the top-level containers.

Work queues are unbounded, so claimed back-pressure does not exist

`FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates each `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (line 185), and `submit()` (`work_queue.put(work_item)`) never blocks or applies any limit. The class docstrings for `FixedQueuePool` and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` explicitly claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up,' but since the queues are unbounded, a single slow/stuck group (which this PR's description cites as the motivating problem) will cause its queue to grow without bound while the main consumer thread keeps accepting and enqueuing new messages. This can lead to unbounded memory growth (queued `WorkItem`s also retain the original `Message` object) and an ever-growing `OffsetTracker.all_offsets`/`outstanding` set, defeating the stated goal of avoiding backlog/parallelism problems.

Because four variable-length segments (action, name, parent) are concatenated with the same separator, different combinations of these values that happen to contain "_" (or produce the same concatenated string through different splits) can collide into the same cache key, returning a cached allow/deny decision for the wrong resource. While action strings and most Kubernetes names are unlikely to contain underscores today, this is a fragile key-construction pattern that silently depends on that external invariant holding.

false_positives.candidate:
Negative results no longer short-circuited by the main permission cache, risking repeated DB round-trips per distinct resource

Previously, a cached permission map that didn't grant access to a specific resource was enough to return 'denied' without hitting the DB. Now, any cache hit that evaluates to 'not allowed' triggers an unconditional DB refetch of full identity permissions (getIdentityPermissions) before the result can be cached per-resource in permDenialCache. For a legitimately-denied identity, every distinct (name, parentFolder) combination requested during the permDenialCache TTL window (30s) incurs one full DB permission query (basic role + teams + permissions) the first time it's seen, since the per-resource denial cache has not yet been populated for that specific resource/folder pair. A client enumerating many resource names (or polling many different items the user has no access to) can therefore generate significant extra DB load compared to before this change.

Permission-denial cache can reintroduce the exact staleness bug the PR is meant to fix

In Check(), after the early permDenialCache short-circuit (lines 116-121), a negative Check() result (resource not found in the cached permission map) causes a fresh DB query and, if still denied, a new entry is written to permDenialCache with shortCacheTTL (30s) (lines 153-155). If any Check() call is evaluated for a given (user, action, name, parentFolder) tuple shortly before the underlying resource becomes visible/granted (e.g. a speculative/early access check, or a check issued immediately after creation but before permissions/propagation settle), that negative result is now cached explicitly for up to 30s and will short-circuit all subsequent checks for that exact resource during that window — even though the resource now exists and the user should be allowed. This can resurrect, in a narrower but still real window, the exact 'user can't access the item they just created' problem this PR is meant to solve, because the explicit denial cache is not invalidated when the underlying permission/permCache is refreshed.

permissionCacheUsage metric mislabels cache hits that end up denied as cache misses

When getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cached permission map (err == nil) but checkPermission on it returns false, the code does not record a cache hit; it falls through to line 137 which unconditionally increments permissionCacheUsage with label "false" (cache miss), even though the cache was actually consulted and hit. This understates the true cache hit rate for any action whose cached permission set does not include the requested resource, which will skew cache-hit-rate dashboards/alerts used to tune cache TTLs or diagnose cache effectiveness.

Although the values originate from fetchIDs (trusted int64 database IDs) rather than external user input, this pattern departs from parameterized-query best practice used elsewhere in the same function and is worth tightening (e.g. chunking into sub-batches of <=999 parameterized placeholders) to avoid any future risk if this code path is ever reused with less-trusted input.

Between the two round-trips, a row that matched the original condition (e.g. an annotation older than the cutoff, or one past the max-count threshold) could be concurrently updated (e.g. via Update(), which changes `epoch`/`epoch_end`/`updated`) so that it no longer satisfies the cleanup criteria, yet it will still be deleted because deleteByIDs only filters on `id IN (...)` without re-validating the original condition. In the goroutines for Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection, the error returned from the Legacy store call (e.g. `errObjectSt` in Create) is only fed into `recordLegacyDuration`/`recordStorageDuration` as a boolean; it is never logged (e.g. via `log.Error(...)`). Previously (pre-PR) these failures were logged with contextual detail. Since these writes now happen asynchronously and their result is not surfaced to the caller at all, silently dropping the error message removes the only way an operator could discover/debug data divergence between Legacy and Unified storage, beyond a boolean metric increment.

Async legacy writes derive from the request-scoped context, which is canceled once the handler returns

In Create (and similarly in Delete line 110, Update line 135, and DeleteCollection line 163), the goroutine that performs the asynchronous Legacy write does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` using the `ctx` that was passed into the outer method, i.e. the request's context. The outer function returns immediately after the Storage write succeeds (it does not wait for the goroutine), so the HTTP handler completes and the underlying request context is typically canceled by the server right after the response is sent. Because the 10s timeout context is derived from (a child of) that request context, it will also be canceled as soon as the parent is canceled, aborting the legacy write before it has a chance to run or complete. This defeats the entire purpose of Mode 3's 'best effort' async legacy write, since legacy writes will routinely fail with context-canceled errors instead of actually persisting data. A decoupled context (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh context carrying only the needed values) should be used as the parent for the goroutine's timeout context.

Mode3 tests never verify that the asynchronous legacy write actually occurs

TestMode3_Create (and similarly TestMode3_Delete, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_DeleteCollection) set up `m.On("Create"/"Delete"/"Update"/"DeleteCollection", ...)` expectations on the legacy mock, but since the real implementation now fires the legacy write in a goroutine, the test function can return before the goroutine executes. The tests never call `m.AssertExpectations(t)` / `m.AssertCalled(t, ...)` nor synchronize with the goroutine (e.g. via a channel/WaitGroup), so the test will pass whether or not the legacy write ever runs or succeeds. When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. The same bug exists in `Update` (line 129) where a Storage.Update failure is also recorded via `recordLegacyDuration` instead of `recordStorageDuration`.

The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

Every goroutine that passed the initial RLock-based nil check will proceed to recompute the result (reading the manifest file or hitting the CDN) even though another goroutine may have just finished populating the cache. Under concurrent initial access (e.g. many simultaneous requests hitting GetWebAssets before the cache is warm), this causes redundant file reads and, worse, redundant outbound HTTP requests to the CDN in readWebAssetsFromCDN, which is both wasteful and could amplify load on an external CDN endpoint.

The PR fixes a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache variable but does not add any test (e.g. a test exercising GetWebAssets concurrently, ideally run with -race) to verify the fix or guard against future regressions. Without such a test, a future refactor could easily reintroduce the race undetected.

The entryPointAssetsCacheMu write lock (acquired at line 48 and released via defer at line 49) is held for the entire duration of readWebAssetsFromFile/readWebAssetsFromCDN, including a network round-trip when a CDN URL is configured. While this does fix the data race, it means every concurrent call to GetWebAssets that misses the cache (or is in Dev mode, which always recomputes) will serialize behind a potentially slow network call, which can increase request latency under load compared to a design that only locks around the shared variable assignment.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the backend-wide lock around BuildIndex allows duplicate/corrupting concurrent builds for the same key

Previously bleveBackend.BuildIndex held cacheMu.Lock() for the entire function (including running the builder callback that populates the index), which serialized all builds. This PR removes that lock and only takes cacheMu briefly at the very end to insert into b.cache. getOrCreateIndex() in search.go checks GetIndex() for a cached entry and, if absent, calls build()/BuildIndex() -- there is no synchronization preventing two concurrent callers for the *same* NamespacedResource key from both seeing a cache miss and both calling BuildIndex concurrently. For disk-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold), two goroutines would call bleve.New(dir, mapper) on the same directory concurrently, which can fail or corrupt index data; for memory-backed indexes, the loser's bleve.Index is simply overwritten in the cache map and never closed, leaking resources. The intended optimization (finer-grained locking) should still serialize builds per-key (e.g., per-key mutex/singleflight) rather than removing the serialization entirely.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Postgres integration test silently skipped with vague TODO

The newly added skip for the `postgres` dbType disables the only integration test that exercises module server startup with the storage server target against Postgres, with just a TODO comment ('test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.') and no linked issue or root-cause explanation. Given this PR changes resource-server initialization timing (synchronous init at startup) which this very test is meant to validate, losing Postgres coverage reduces confidence that the new startup behavior works correctly on that backend.

Removing per-call Init() checks breaks shutdown gating

Previously every RPC handler (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob) called s.Init(ctx) before doing work. Because Init() uses sync.Once, after the server was already initialized this call cheaply returned the cached s.initErr, which Stop() deliberately sets to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped" to make in-flight and new RPCs fail once shutdown begins. This PR removes all of those Init() calls from the handlers (since init now happens once synchronously in NewResourceServer), but Stop() still mutates s.initErr and nothing reads it anymore. As a result, after Stop() is called, handlers (including IsHealthy, used for liveness/readiness) no longer reflect the stopped state and will keep processing requests normally until the underlying resources themselves start failing, defeating the graceful-shutdown mechanism that existed before this change.

Swapped order of watcher init and search init can drop events in HA setups

Init() previously started the broadcaster watcher (initWatcher) before building the search index; this PR swaps the order so the (potentially long-running) search.init() runs first and initWatcher() runs only after it completes. The main broadcaster's starting resource version is determined at the moment initWatcher() calls WatchWriteEvents, so any WriteEvents produced by other instances during the lengthy index-build window (explicitly a supported HA scenario per StorageBackend's WatchWriteEvents doc: 'For HA setups, this will be more events than the local WriteEvent above!') will not be observed by this instance's broadcaster and will be missed by clients subscribing via Watch() once the server comes up. This should be verified/tested, since it directly affects correctness of the watch stream in multi-replica deployments.

Synchronous, unbounded Init() in NewResourceServer can block startup indefinitely

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously before returning, and the ctx passed in is derived from context.Background() with no deadline. Init() runs s.search.init(ctx), which builds the full search index over every namespace found via GetResourceStats — the exact operation the PR says 'takes too long' inside a gRPC call's context. Moving this work earlier removes the gRPC-context-cancellation symptom, but now the entire module/server construction blocks for however long indexing takes, with no timeout or cancellation path exposed to the caller. In orchestrated environments this can cause startup/readiness probes to fail or force restarts before initialization completes, and there's no way for an operator to bound or cancel this work.

In searchSupport.init(), totalBatchesIndexed++ and the outer err variable (declared from `stats, err := s.storage.GetResourceStats(...)`) are both written inside group.Go closures that run concurrently (errgroup limited to s.initWorkers, which can be >1). Both totalBatchesIndexed and err are shared, non-atomic variables written from multiple goroutines without any mutex/atomic, which is a data race (will be flagged by `go test -race`) and can produce an incorrect/non-deterministic final totalBatchesIndexed count used in the trace span attribute, and a lost/overwritten err value. Given this PR's explicit goal of increasing indexing concurrency, this race becomes more likely to actually manifest and should be fixed (e.g., use atomic counters and let errgroup.Wait() be the sole source of the returned error).

Login cache invalidation always clears all FetchModes regardless of relevance

registerIDPLoginInvalidation() and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() both iterate over all FetchMode values and invalidate cacheKeyForLogin for REALM_ONLY, ORG_ONLY and ALL whenever any login-eligibility-affecting change occurs, even if the change only affects one mode (e.g., a realm-only IDP toggling enabled state cannot possibly affect the ORG_ONLY cache, yet that cache is invalidated and must be rebuilt anyway). This causes unnecessary cache rebuilds for unrelated fetch modes on every qualifying create/update/remove operation, which could be avoided by selecting the specific FetchMode(s) impacted by the change.

remove() now always performs an extra unconditional storage lookup

`remove(String alias)` now unconditionally calls `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` at the top of the method to obtain `storedIdp`, even in the branch where the entry is already present in cache (`cached != null`, lines 105-108) and `cached.getIdentityProvider()` is used instead for the invalidation logic. Previously, the delegate lookup only happened when the cache entry was invalid. This adds an unnecessary database round-trip to every call to remove(), even when cache data is readily available, which is a performance regression on a path that previously avoided redundant delegate queries.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() does not return a BouncyCastle provider, violating the interface contract

CryptoProvider#getBouncyCastleProvider() is documented as returning 'BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider'. This implementation instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is simply whatever JCA provider implements the platform default keystore type (e.g. the JDK's built-in PKCS12 provider), not BouncyCastle at all. Any caller relying on the documented contract (e.g. to register BC-specific algorithms, or pass 'BC' as a provider name) will get unexpected/incorrect behavior rather than a clear UnsupportedOperationException like the rest of the unimplemented methods in this class.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code: throwaway ASN1Encoder instances created and discarded

In concatenatedRSToASN1DER(), lines 114-115 create two separate ASN1Encoder instances and call write(rBigInteger)/write(sBigInteger) on them, but the results are never used (new encoders are created again a few lines later to actually build the returned bytes). This is dead code left over from development that performs unnecessary work on every signature conversion and is confusing to maintain; it should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks binary/source compatibility for existing CryptoProvider implementors

The interface CryptoProvider now declares `int order();` as an abstract method with no default implementation. Any existing third-party or custom implementation of CryptoProvider (e.g. custom SPI providers maintained outside this PR) will fail to compile/load until updated to implement order(). Since CryptoProvider is a public SPI loaded via ServiceLoader, this is a breaking API change that should either provide a default method (e.g. default int order() { return 0; }) or be called out explicitly as a breaking change in release notes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
AuthzClient.create() triggers global static CryptoIntegration initialization as a side effect

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). CryptoIntegration keeps a process-wide static singleton (cryptoProvider) that, once set, cannot be changed except via explicit setProvider(). If AuthzClient.create() is invoked before the hosting application performs its own CryptoIntegration.init() (e.g. when authz-client is embedded inside a larger application/server that shares the same classloader or class-loading hierarchy), the singleton can get permanently locked to whatever CryptoProvider is visible to AuthzClient's classloader at that moment — potentially the minimal AuthzClientCryptoProvider, which throws UnsupportedOperationException for almost every operation except order(), getBouncyCastleProvider(), getEcdsaCryptoProvider() and getKeyStore(). Any later, unrelated code path in the same classloader that needs other crypto features (PEM utils, certificate utils, key generation, etc.) would then fail with UnsupportedOperationException instead of using the application's intended full-featured provider.

No test coverage for the new multi-provider ordering/tie-breaking logic

This PR introduces a significant behavioral change to CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(): instead of failing when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are found, it now sorts by CryptoProvider.order() and silently picks the highest. No unit test is added anywhere in the diff to verify this sorting logic, the tie-breaking behavior when two providers share the same order value, or that a provider is correctly ignored/logged. Given this is core logic that determines which cryptographic backend the whole application uses, it should have direct test coverage.

Removed fail-fast check for multiple CryptoProviders on classpath, now silently resolved with non-deterministic tie-breaking

Previously detectProvider() threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classloader, which protected against misconfiguration (e.g. accidentally having both a FIPS and a non-FIPS provider on the classpath, which has real compliance/security implications). Now the providers are simply sorted by order() and the highest-order one is silently picked, logging the rest only at debug level (logger.debugf, line ~69). If two providers happen to have the same order() value (e.g. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all use order()==200), the choice between them depends on ServiceLoader enumeration order, which is unspecified and can vary across JVMs/classloaders. This can silently select a FIPS or non-FIPS provider unintentionally, with no error raised and only a debug-level log that is typically not visible in production, defeating the original safety check.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Role/client/group removal cleanup listener now gated by the V1 feature flag only

The ProviderEventListener body that disables permissions for a removed role/client/group (calling management(...).roles()/.clients()/.groups().setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)) used to run unconditionally. This PR wraps the whole block in `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))`, i.e. it now only runs when the (older) V1 fine-grained-authz feature is enabled. The `management(...)` factory itself selects V1 vs V2 based on `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2`, so if a deployment only enables the V2 feature (without V1), this cleanup listener will be skipped entirely and permission/resource cleanup for deleted roles/clients/groups will no longer happen for V2 permissions. This change is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (adding Clients resource type) and is not covered by any new test.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission cannot find per-client resources and leaks the catch-all resource name

`getClientsWithPermission` looks up resources via `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)`, which filters on the resource's `type` attribute. However, `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` (used to create the per-client resource when a scoped permission is created for a specific client) never calls `resource.setType(...)`; only the catch-all 'all-resource' entry created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.init()` has its type set to `CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE`. As a result: (1) individual per-client resources will never be returned by `findByType`, so clients with a specific scoped permission are silently omitted from the result set, and (2) if the catch-all 'Clients' resource itself has the scope granted, its resource name ('Clients') is incorrectly added to the returned set as if it were a client id. Any caller treating the returned set as a list of client ids will get wrong/empty results.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No migration path to add the new Clients resource/scopes for realms that already enabled admin permissions

`init()` only creates the schema resources/scopes (including the newly added 'Clients' resource type and its scopes) when `realm.getAdminPermissionsClient()` is null, i.e. only the very first time admin permissions are enabled for a realm. For any realm that already had admin fine-grained permissions (V2) enabled before this change was deployed, `init()` returns immediately and the 'Clients' resource/scope set is never created. Consequently, `ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(...)` will call `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(..., CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE)`, which returns null because the resource doesn't exist, and that null is then passed into `authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)`, risking an NPE (or at least silently returning no permissions) for any existing realm upgrading to this version. There is no migration/upgrade step shown to retrofit existing admin-permission-enabled realms with the new resource type.

Missing test for feature-disabled path on the 'check' subcommand

testFeatureNotEnabled only exercises UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.NAME without the rolling-updates feature enabled. The same feature-gating logic was also added to UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run() (in UpdateCompatibilityCheck.java), but there is no corresponding test verifying that running 'check' without the feature enabled prints the expected error and exits with CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED. Operator enforcement of rolling-updates feature flag not verifiable in this change set

The new CAUTION block states 'While on preview stage, the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail.' However, none of the files included in this PR implement an operator-side check that fails when the update stanza is used without the feature enabled (only the CLI update-compatibility commands gained such a check in AbstractUpdatesCommand/UpdateCompatibilityCheck/Metadata). ROLLING_UPDATES feature auto-enables with the generic 'preview' profile

Per Profile.isEnabledByDefault(), any Type.PREVIEW feature is automatically turned on whenever the server-wide profile is set to PREVIEW (e.g. via a general '--profile=preview' or env var toggle), without the operator/administrator explicitly opting into 'rolling-updates'. true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants management rights to callers that only have VIEW scope on groups

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (no-arg, used e.g. by GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() via auth.groups().requireManage()) is implemented as:

    return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);

This is an exact copy of canView()'s scope list. As a result, an admin who was only granted the VIEW scope on the all-groups resource (and not MANAGE) is treated as being allowed to manage (create/update) groups, because hasPermission() returns true as soon as any of the listed scopes is granted. canManage(GroupModel) correctly checks only AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, which highlights that the no-arg canManage() is inconsistent/incorrect. This is a privilege-escalation bug: a read-only group permission effectively becomes a write permission for top-level group management. No test exercises a VIEW-only permission against a management action, so this regression is not caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() uses the resource's internal id instead of the group's id, breaking per-group view filtering

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), for each group-type Resource found, the code calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) and adds groupResource.getId() to the granted set. However, resources created for groups via AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() store the actual GroupModel id in resource.getName() (see resolveGroup()), not in resource.getId() (which is the authorization store's own generated identifier for the Resource entity). All other methods in this class (canView(GroupModel), canManage(GroupModel), canViewMembers, canManageMembers, canManageMembership) correctly pass group.getId() which matches resource.getName(). Because hasPermission()'s internal lookup does resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId), passing the resource's own id instead of its name will almost never find the resource, so permission checks for individual groups silently fail and fall back to the (usually absent) all-groups permission. Additionally, even where hasPermission did succeed, the method would return the wrong identifiers (resource ids, not group ids) in the resulting Set<String>. Since this set is used by UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource to filter the user search by group membership (session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, groupIds)), real group ids never show up there, so admins granted per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions will not see any users through this path, defeating the feature added by this PR (the exact scenario covered by GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest#testCanViewUserByViewGroupMembers / testCanViewUserByManageGroupMembers).

false_positives.candidate:
No negative test ensures VIEW-only group permission cannot perform management actions

testManageAllGroups() only exercises the case where the policy is granted the MANAGE scope and verifies group creation/management succeeds. There is no test that grants only the VIEW scope for all-groups (or a specific group) and asserts that management actions (create group, add child, map roles) are forbidden. Given the canManage() bug in GroupPermissionsV2 (treats VIEW as sufficient for MANAGE), such a negative test would have caught the privilege-escalation regression before merge.

getResourceName() has no special-cased display for Groups (or Clients) resource type

getResourceName() special-cases USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE to resolve a friendly name ("All users" or the username) for display purposes (e.g. in the admin console permission UI). No equivalent handling was added for the newly introduced GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE (or for CLIENTS), so for group-scoped permissions the method falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which for individually-scoped group permissions is the raw group UUID (the resource name) rather than a human-readable group name/path. This is inconsistent with the Users handling added in the same method and will show opaque IDs instead of group names wherever this helper is used to render permission resource names.

The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
ANCHOR_PATTERN overly broad, matches tags other than anchors

ANCHOR_PATTERN = Pattern.compile("</?a[^>]*>") matches any tag whose name starts with the letter 'a' (e.g. '<address>', '<abbr>'), not just '<a>' anchor tags, because '[^>]*' allows any following characters. This can cause santizeAnchors() to mislabel and process non-anchor tags as if they were anchors, producing a misleading 'Didn't find anchor tag' message for tags that are not actually anchors.

HTML sanitizer policies rebuilt for every file instance

POLICY_SOME_HTML and POLICY_NO_HTML are non-static instance fields rebuilt via HtmlPolicyBuilder().toFactory() every time a VerifyMessageProperties object is constructed (i.e., once per properties file being verified). Since these policies are stateless and identical across all files, they should be static final fields shared across instances, avoiding unnecessary object construction for every theme message file scanned.

ICU MessageFormat choice syntax injected into i18next (double-brace) translation file

The value for 'error-invalid-multivalued-size' was changed from 'Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).' to 'Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.'. Every other key in this file (and the whole account-ui/admin-ui message bundle) uses i18next's double-curly-brace interpolation syntax ({{0}}) and i18next pluralization suffixes (e.g. resourceSharedWith_one/_zero/_other), not Java's single-brace MessageFormat/ChoiceFormat. react-i18next does not interpret '{0,choice,...}' syntax, so the UI will render the literal unprocessed string instead of a correctly pluralized sentence. This appears to be the Java-theme fix (which is appropriate for FreeMarker/MessageFormat-based themes) mistakenly applied to the JS UI translation bundle as well.

Lithuanian login translation replaced with Italian text

loginTotpStep1 was changed to 'Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:' which is Italian, not Lithuanian, when removing the disallowed anchor tags. This is a content/locale regression introduced while fixing the HTML sanitization issue; the replacement text should be a correct Lithuanian translation.

Missing/unreadable English reference file crashes the whole build instead of reporting a validation error

verifySafeHtml() computes the path of the English reference file via a brittle string-replace heuristic (replacing "resources-community" with "resources" and the locale suffix with "_en.properties"), then wraps any IOException from reading it in an unchecked RuntimeException (lines 76-80). Because verify() only catches IOException, this RuntimeException propagates uncaught out of verify(), aborting the whole Maven build with a raw stack trace instead of producing a MojoExecutionException or an entry in the returned messages list. Since theme-verifier-maven-plugin is packaged as a general-purpose plugin, any theme/module whose directory layout doesn't match this exact convention (or that lacks an '_en' counterpart) will crash the build rather than fail gracefully with an actionable message.

No tests cover the hardcoded per-key normalization exceptions

normalizeValue() hardcodes special handling for specific keys ('templateHelp', 'optimizeLookupHelp', and keys starting with 'linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit' or equal to 'error-invalid-multivalued-size') to avoid false-positive HTML/illegal-tag detections caused by legitimate '<NAME>'/'<Extensions>'/ChoiceFormat syntax. None of the added tests exercise these branches, so regressions in this fragile, key-name-based allowlist (e.g. a new key using '{0,choice,...}' syntax not added to the list) would silently be flagged as illegal HTML with no test coverage to catch it.

Same ICU choice-format regression applied to Admin UI i18next messages

error-invalid-multivalued-size was changed from the i18next double-brace form 'Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).' to a Java ChoiceFormat string 'Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.'. This file feeds the React admin console (i18next), which uses {{var}} interpolation and _one/_other plural key suffixes, not inline ChoiceFormat syntax. The new string will be displayed verbatim to admins instead of being properly interpolated/pluralized, breaking this specific validation error message in the Admin Console UI.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate null-check validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId

In the constructor:
```
Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null grantType not allowed");
Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");
```
The second call re-checks `grantType` again (with a misleading message about `rawTokenId`) instead of checking `rawTokenId`. Consequently, a null `rawTokenId` is never rejected. Downstream, `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId()` concatenates `tokenContext.getRawTokenId()` directly into the token id string; if it is null, the resulting access token id will literally contain the string "null" instead of a real token id, corrupting token uniqueness/identity instead of failing fast with a clear error.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId() matcher has wrong substring offset and inverted comparison logic

In `isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)`, the matcher does:
```
if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;
```
Two separate bugs here:
1. The grant-type shortcut occupies characters 4-6 of the 6-character context prefix (positions `[4,6)`), not `[3,5)`. For a token id like `onrtac:...`, `substring(3,5)` yields `"ta"`, not the grant shortcut `"ac"`.
2. Even ignoring the offset bug, the condition is inverted: the method should return `false` (fail the match) when the shortcut does NOT equal the expected value, but it currently returns `false` only when it DOES equal it.

As a result, this matcher almost never fails regardless of which grant type is actually encoded in the token id (since `substring(3,5)` virtually never matches `expectedGrantShortcut`, the `if` never triggers and the method falls through to `isUUID()` on the raw id, effectively ignoring the grant-type check entirely). All tests using `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, `expectAuthReqIdToToken`, etc. that rely on this matcher do not actually verify the new token-id encoding feature, defeating the purpose of the added assertions and potentially masking real encoding bugs.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Javadoc for getShortcut() contradicts the fixed 2-character format enforced by the encoder

The javadoc states: "@return usually like 3-letters shortcut of specific grants ... Shortcut should be unique across grants." However, `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider`/`DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory` hard-code a fixed 2-character length for the grant-type segment (e.g. `encodedContext.substring(4, 6)` and the overall length check `encodedContext.length() != 6`). All built-in grant factories indeed return exactly 2 characters, which contradicts the "3-letters" documentation. If a developer follows the javadoc and implements a 3-character shortcut for a custom grant type, the fixed-length assumptions in the encoder will break (the encoder will produce malformed ids, and decoding of its own just-generated token ids will throw IllegalArgumentException due to the length-6 check).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
Access token jti format change is an unannounced/unflagged contract change with no opt-out

`initToken()` now always runs the generated token id through `TokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId()`, changing the shape of the `jti` claim for every access token from a plain UUID to a prefixed value like `onrtac:<uuid>`. Any external tooling, logging/correlation systems, or internal code (admin REST API, introspection consumers, custom SPI implementations) that assumes the access token id is a canonical UUID (e.g. checks length 36, applies UUID regex, or compares it against other UUID-shaped identifiers) will now break. There is no configuration flag/toggle shown to disable this new encoding for backward-compatibility, and no migration note is provided for deployments relying on the previous token id format.

New abstract method added to existing provider factory interface without a default implementation

`getShortcut()` is added as a new abstract method on `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory`, which extends `ProviderFactory`. Any existing custom/third-party implementation of this SPI (e.g. a custom grant type extension) will now fail to compile/deploy until it implements this new method, since no default implementation is provided. Given this is meant to be an extensible SPI (the PR description explicitly states "provider adds ability for someone to introduce his own provider"), this is a breaking change for existing extensions without a deprecation/default-method migration path.

No validation that OAuth2GrantTypeFactory shortcuts are exactly 2 characters, risking self-generated tokens becoming undecodable

`postInit()` collects grant-type shortcuts from all `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` implementations without verifying their length. `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId()` simply concatenates the session/token/grant shortcuts assuming each is exactly 2 characters, and `getTokenContextFromTokenId()` enforces a strict 6-character total length for decoding. If any (built-in or third-party) `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` implementation returns a shortcut that isn't exactly 2 characters (which the javadoc actually suggests is acceptable, e.g. 3 characters), tokens generated with that grant type will fail decoding later (e.g. in introspection or revocation code paths that call `getTokenContextFromTokenId`), throwing `IllegalArgumentException("Incorrect token id ... Duplicate null-check validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId

In the constructor:
```
Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null grantType not allowed");
Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");
```
The second call re-checks `grantType` again (with a misleading message about `rawTokenId`) instead of checking `rawTokenId`. Consequently, a null `rawTokenId` is never rejected. Downstream, `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId()` concatenates `tokenContext.getRawTokenId()` directly into the token id string; if it is null, the resulting access token id will literally contain the string "null" instead of a real token id, corrupting token uniqueness/identity instead of failing fast with a clear error.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId() matcher has wrong substring offset and inverted comparison logic

In `isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)`, the matcher does:
```
if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;
```
Two separate bugs here:
1. The grant-type shortcut occupies characters 4-6 of the 6-character context prefix (positions `[4,6)`), not `[3,5)`. For a token id like `onrtac:...`, `substring(3,5)` yields `"ta"`, not the grant shortcut `"ac"`.
2. Even ignoring the offset bug, the condition is inverted: the method should return `false` (fail the match) when the shortcut does NOT equal the expected value, but it currently returns `false` only when it DOES equal it.

As a result, this matcher almost never fails regardless of which grant type is actually encoded in the token id (since `substring(3,5)` virtually never matches `expectedGrantShortcut`, the `if` never triggers and the method falls through to `isUUID()` on the raw id, effectively ignoring the grant-type check entirely). All tests using `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, `expectAuthReqIdToToken`, etc. that rely on this matcher do not actually verify the new token-id encoding feature, defeating the purpose of the added assertions and potentially masking real encoding bugs.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same two bugs in `isAccessTokenId` as the golden comment: the incorrect substring indices (`(3, 5)` instead of `(4, 6)`) and the inverted equality check returning `false` on a match.

No validation that OAuth2GrantTypeFactory shortcuts are exactly 2 characters, risking self-generated tokens becoming undecodable

`postInit()` collects grant-type shortcuts from all `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` implementations without verifying their length. `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId()` simply concatenates the session/token/grant shortcuts assuming each is exactly 2 characters, and `getTokenContextFromTokenId()` enforces a strict 6-character total length for decoding. If any (built-in or third-party) `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` implementation returns a shortcut that isn't exactly 2 characters (which the javadoc actually suggests is acceptable, e.g. 3 characters), tokens generated with that grant type will fail decoding later (e.g. in introspection or revocation code paths that call `getTokenContextFromTokenId`), throwing `IllegalArgumentException("Incorrect token id ... Expected length of 6")` for tokens the server itself just issued.

New abstract method added to existing provider factory interface without a default implementation

`getShortcut()` is added as a new abstract method on `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory`, which extends `ProviderFactory`. Any existing custom/third-party implementation of this SPI (e.g. a custom grant type extension) will now fail to compile/deploy until it implements this new method, since no default implementation is provided. Given this is meant to be an extensible SPI (the PR description explicitly states "provider adds ability for someone to introduce his own provider"), this is a breaking change for existing extensions without a deprecation/default-method migration path.

Access token jti format change is an unannounced/unflagged contract change with no opt-out

`initToken()` now always runs the generated token id through `TokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId()`, changing the shape of the `jti` claim for every access token from a plain UUID to a prefixed value like `onrtac:<uuid>`. Any external tooling, logging/correlation systems, or internal code (admin REST API, introspection consumers, custom SPI implementations) that assumes the access token id is a canonical UUID (e.g. checks length 36, applies UUID regex, or compares it against other UUID-shaped identifiers) will now break. There is no configuration flag/toggle shown to disable this new encoding for backward-compatibility, and no migration note is provided for deployments relying on the previous token id format.

false_positives.candidate:
Recovery codes stored in user storage have no one-time-use tracking

isValid() for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE only checks whether the submitted code exists in the stored raw list (`generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(...)`) and never removes/marks the matching code as used, nor is there any subsequent call anywhere in the authentication flow (RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.action) that writes back a 'used' state to the user-storage provider after a successful login. Since getCredentials()/isValid() always reconstruct the credential model from the same unchanged raw code list stored in credentialData, every recovery code remains valid forever for users whose recovery codes live in this storage provider, defeating the single-use guarantee that recovery codes are supposed to provide. This is a real security/data-integrity regression introduced together with the feature that lets recovery codes be created in user storage, and the reference provider shipped in this PR demonstrates the gap without addressing it.

getCredentials() can NPE when user is not found in the backing map

getCredentials(RealmModel, UserModel) calls `var myUser = getMyUser(user);` and then immediately dereferences `myUser.recoveryCodes` without a null check. Every other method in this class that uses getMyUser() (e.g. getDisableableCredentialTypesStream, isConfiguredFor) explicitly guards against `myUser == null` before accessing its fields. If getMyUser returns null here (user removed concurrently, race, or lookup inconsistency), this will throw a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty/partial credential stream.

Raw (unhashed) recovery codes are forwarded to the user-storage provider

createRecoveryCodesCredential builds `UserCredentialModel recoveryCodesCredential` from `recoveryCodesJson`, which is the plain JSON serialization of the raw generated codes (`generatedCodes`), not the hashed representation used by `credentialModel` for local storage. This value is passed verbatim to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`, which the companion test provider (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage) stores and compares as-is, i.e. in plaintext. Unlike the local-DB path where RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel stores hashed codes, any user-storage implementation that persists the UserCredentialModel's challenge response directly (as the shipped reference implementation does) will store one-time recovery codes unhashed at rest, weakening the security of the feature for federated users.

removeStoredCredentialById likely cannot remove a user-storage-backed recovery codes credential

When all recovery codes have been used, the code calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`. For credentials that are now newly supported to live in user storage (per this PR), the id returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() comes from the federated provider (e.g. a synthetic id generated by the test storage provider), not from the local credential store. removeStoredCredentialById is historically scoped to credentials persisted in the local DB store; it is not guaranteed to propagate removal to an external UserStorageProvider. Consequently the exhausted recovery-codes credential may silently remain configured in the user-storage provider even though the authenticator believes it removed it, leaving a stale/exhausted credential rather than cleanly forcing re-setup.

No test coverage for recovery-code exhaustion/removal or disabling when stored in user storage

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only exercises generating recovery codes and performing a single successful login with one code against the new user-storage-backed credential path. There is no test verifying that codes become single-use (cannot be reused), that the credential is properly removed/replaced once all codes are consumed, or that admin/account REST credential disable operations behave correctly for a recovery-codes credential stored in user storage (unlike the analogous OTP tests testDisableCredentialsInUserStorage / testOTPSetupAndRemoveThroughAccountMgmtAndLogin). Given the new behavior this PR introduces, these scenarios should be covered to catch regressions like unlimited code reuse.

false_positives.candidate:
Removed fail-fast check for multiple CryptoProviders on classpath, now silently resolved with non-deterministic tie-breaking

Previously detectProvider() threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classloader, which protected against misconfiguration (e.g. accidentally having both a FIPS and a non-FIPS provider on the classpath, which has real compliance/security implications). Now the providers are simply sorted by order() and the highest-order one is silently picked, logging the rest only at debug level (logger.debugf, line ~69). If two providers happen to have the same order() value (e.g. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all use order()==200), the choice between them depends on ServiceLoader enumeration order, which is unspecified and can vary across JVMs/classloaders. This can silently select a FIPS or non-FIPS provider unintentionally, with no error raised and only a debug-level log that is typically not visible in production, defeating the original safety check.

AuthzClient.create() triggers global static CryptoIntegration initialization as a side effect

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). CryptoIntegration keeps a process-wide static singleton (cryptoProvider) that, once set, cannot be changed except via explicit setProvider(). If AuthzClient.create() is invoked before the hosting application performs its own CryptoIntegration.init() (e.g. when authz-client is embedded inside a larger application/server that shares the same classloader or class-loading hierarchy), the singleton can get permanently locked to whatever CryptoProvider is visible to AuthzClient's classloader at that moment — potentially the minimal AuthzClientCryptoProvider, which throws UnsupportedOperationException for almost every operation except order(), getBouncyCastleProvider(), getEcdsaCryptoProvider() and getKeyStore(). Any later, unrelated code path in the same classloader that needs other crypto features (PEM utils, certificate utils, key generation, etc.) would then fail with UnsupportedOperationException instead of using the application's intended full-featured provider.

No test coverage for the new multi-provider ordering/tie-breaking logic

This PR introduces a significant behavioral change to CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(): instead of failing when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are found, it now sorts by CryptoProvider.order() and silently picks the highest. No unit test is added anywhere in the diff to verify this sorting logic, the tie-breaking behavior when two providers share the same order value, or that a provider is correctly ignored/logged. Given this is core logic that determines which cryptographic backend the whole application uses, it should have direct test coverage.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the backend-wide lock around BuildIndex allows duplicate/corrupting concurrent builds for the same key

Previously bleveBackend.BuildIndex held cacheMu.Lock() for the entire function (including running the builder callback that populates the index), which serialized all builds. This PR removes that lock and only takes cacheMu briefly at the very end to insert into b.cache. getOrCreateIndex() in search.go checks GetIndex() for a cached entry and, if absent, calls build()/BuildIndex() -- there is no synchronization preventing two concurrent callers for the *same* NamespacedResource key from both seeing a cache miss and both calling BuildIndex concurrently. For disk-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold), two goroutines would call bleve.New(dir, mapper) on the same directory concurrently, which can fail or corrupt index data; for memory-backed indexes, the loser's bleve.Index is simply overwritten in the cache map and never closed, leaking resources. The intended optimization (finer-grained locking) should still serialize builds per-key (e.g., per-key mutex/singleflight) rather than removing the serialization entirely.

false_positives.candidate:
Removing per-call Init() checks breaks shutdown gating

Previously every RPC handler (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob) called s.Init(ctx) before doing work. Because Init() uses sync.Once, after the server was already initialized this call cheaply returned the cached s.initErr, which Stop() deliberately sets to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped" to make in-flight and new RPCs fail once shutdown begins. This PR removes all of those Init() calls from the handlers (since init now happens once synchronously in NewResourceServer), but Stop() still mutates s.initErr and nothing reads it anymore. As a result, after Stop() is called, handlers (including IsHealthy, used for liveness/readiness) no longer reflect the stopped state and will keep processing requests normally until the underlying resources themselves start failing, defeating the graceful-shutdown mechanism that existed before this change.

Synchronous, unbounded Init() in NewResourceServer can block startup indefinitely

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously before returning, and the ctx passed in is derived from context.Background() with no deadline. Init() runs s.search.init(ctx), which builds the full search index over every namespace found via GetResourceStats — the exact operation the PR says 'takes too long' inside a gRPC call's context. Moving this work earlier removes the gRPC-context-cancellation symptom, but now the entire module/server construction blocks for however long indexing takes, with no timeout or cancellation path exposed to the caller. In orchestrated environments this can cause startup/readiness probes to fail or force restarts before initialization completes, and there's no way for an operator to bound or cancel this work.

Unsynchronized shared variables mutated by concurrent errgroup goroutines

In searchSupport.init(), totalBatchesIndexed++ and the outer err variable (declared from `stats, err := s.storage.GetResourceStats(...)`) are both written inside group.Go closures that run concurrently (errgroup limited to s.initWorkers, which can be >1). Both totalBatchesIndexed and err are shared, non-atomic variables written from multiple goroutines without any mutex/atomic, which is a data race (will be flagged by `go test -race`) and can produce an incorrect/non-deterministic final totalBatchesIndexed count used in the trace span attribute, and a lost/overwritten err value. Given this PR's explicit goal of increasing indexing concurrency, this race becomes more likely to actually manifest and should be fixed (e.g., use atomic counters and let errgroup.Wait() be the sole source of the returned error).

Swapped order of watcher init and search init can drop events in HA setups

Init() previously started the broadcaster watcher (initWatcher) before building the search index; this PR swaps the order so the (potentially long-running) search.init() runs first and initWatcher() runs only after it completes. The main broadcaster's starting resource version is determined at the moment initWatcher() calls WatchWriteEvents, so any WriteEvents produced by other instances during the lengthy index-build window (explicitly a supported HA scenario per StorageBackend's WatchWriteEvents doc: 'For HA setups, this will be more events than the local WriteEvent above!') will not be observed by this instance's broadcaster and will be missed by clients subscribing via Watch() once the server comes up. This should be verified/tested, since it directly affects correctness of the watch stream in multi-replica deployments.

The newly added skip for the `postgres` dbType disables the only integration test that exercises module server startup with the storage server target against Postgres, with just a TODO comment ('test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.') and no linked issue or root-cause explanation. Shared FixedQueuePool is permanently destroyed by per-rebalance strategy close()/terminate()

ResultsStrategyFactory creates a single `FixedQueuePool` instance once in `__init__` (result_consumer.py, inside `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)`), intended to live for the lifetime of the consumer process and be reused across partition rebalances. However, `create_with_partitions` builds a brand-new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` every time it is called (e.g. on every rebalance), and that strategy's `close()`/`terminate()` methods (queue_consumer.py lines 335-342) call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets every worker thread's `shutdown` flag and shuts down every underlying `queue.Queue`. Arroyo calls `close()`/`terminate()` on the active strategy whenever partitions are revoked (which happens on every consumer group rebalance), and then calls `create_with_partitions` again for the new assignment. Because the factory still holds the same (now permanently dead) `queue_pool` object, the new strategy submits work items into queues whose worker threads have already exited, so no further messages are ever processed after the first rebalance - the consumer silently stalls without raising any error, with no new offsets being committed from that point forward.

`FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates each `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (line 185), and `submit()` (`work_queue.put(work_item)`) never blocks or applies any limit. The class docstrings for `FixedQueuePool` and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` explicitly claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up,' but since the queues are unbounded, a single slow/stuck group (which this PR's description cites as the motivating problem) will cause its queue to grow without bound while the main consumer thread keeps accepting and enqueuing new messages. This can lead to unbounded memory growth (queued `WorkItem`s also retain the original `Message` object) and an ever-growing `OffsetTracker.all_offsets`/`outstanding` set, defeating the stated goal of avoiding backlog/parallelism problems.

`OffsetTracker` protects each partition's offset *set* with a per-partition lock, but the outer dictionaries (`all_offsets`, `outstanding`, `last_committed`, `partition_locks`) have no lock guarding structural changes. `get_committable_offsets()` does `for partition in list(self.all_offsets.keys())` (line 74) while `add_offset()` (called from the consumer thread) can concurrently insert a brand-new partition key into the same defaultdict via `self.all_offsets[partition]`. Mutating a dict's size while another thread is iterating/snapshotting its keys can intermittently raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` in CPython, since `add_offset` and `get_committable_offsets`/`mark_committed` run on different threads (main consumer thread vs. the dedicated commit thread) without a shared lock around the top-level containers.

No test coverage for partition revocation/reassignment (rebalance)

None of the new tests in test_queue_consumer.py or the thread-queue-parallel tests added to tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py exercise calling `create_with_partitions` more than once on the same `ResultsStrategyFactory`/`queue_pool`, or calling `close()`/`terminate()` on the returned `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` followed by a second `create_with_partitions` call (which is what happens on a real Kafka consumer group rebalance). This leaves the critical bug where `strategy.close()` kills the shared `FixedQueuePool` permanently (see queue_consumer.py close()/terminate()) completely uncovered by tests, even though rebalances are a normal and frequent occurrence in production Kafka consumers.

Misleading docstring claiming backpressure that doesn't exist

The docstring of `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` (and similarly `FixedQueuePool`) states 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' as a guaranteed property, but the underlying `queue.Queue` objects are created with no `maxsize`, so they never 'fill up' and no backpressure is ever applied to the Kafka consumer. This documentation is inaccurate and could mislead future maintainers into believing memory/backlog growth is bounded when it is not.

addMembers/removeMember actions swallow errors silently

The `addMembers` action (line 61-65) calls `this.get("model").addMembers(this.get("usernames"))` and `removeMember` (line 51-59) calls `self.get("model").removeMember(member)` without attaching a `.catch`/error handler on the returned promise, unlike `save` and `destroy` which do handle rejection with `bootbox.alert`. The backend (`Admin::GroupsController#add_members`/`#remove_member`) returns a 422 with an error message when the group is automatic, or can fail for other reasons (e.g. unknown usernames silently skipped, group save validation failure). Because there is no error handler, any such failure is silently swallowed in the UI and the user gets no feedback that the add/remove operation did not succeed.

`automatic` lookup in item view template resolves against the member, not the group

`group_member.hbs` is rendered as the template for the `group-member` itemView used via `{{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}` in `group.hbs`. Since this is the non-block `{{each}}` form with an `itemView`, the rendering context for each item's template is the member object itself, not the outer group/controller context. The bare `{{#unless automatic}}` check in this template therefore resolves `automatic` against the `member` (a user object, which has no `automatic` property) rather than against the group's `automatic` flag, so it will always be falsy and the remove link will be rendered for members of automatic groups too, even though removal is disallowed server-side. This produces a UI affordance that always fails (compounded by the missing error handling noted elsewhere), misleading admins into thinking they can remove members from automatic groups.

Membership mutation is persisted before validation/save, causing misleading error responses

In `remove_member`, `group.users.delete(user_id)` (line 90) immediately executes a DELETE against the join table for a persisted `group`/association, and in `add_members`, `group.add(user)` (line 73) similarly persists membership immediately via the association. Only afterwards is `group.save` called to determine the HTTP response. If `group.save` fails for any unrelated reason (e.g. stale validation state), the controller renders `render_json_error(group)` even though the membership change has already been committed to the database. Clients receiving an error response will believe the operation failed and may retry, potentially causing duplicate adds or confusing inconsistent state, since the actual membership mutation already succeeded independent of the `save` result.

Unhandled RecordNotFound possible when removing a non-member/invalid user_id

`remove_member` calls `group.users.delete(user_id)` with a raw integer id and no rescue. Depending on how the has_many association's `delete` resolves an id that is not currently part of the group's collection (e.g. stale client state, concurrent removal, or a malicious/incorrect user_id), this can raise `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound`, which is not rescued here and would bubble up as an unhandled 500 error instead of a clean validation error response. There is also no spec covering this scenario (see spec/controllers/admin/groups_controller_spec.rb), so this regression path is untested.

The new code applies a flat default `limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` to all groups regardless of the `automatic` flag. This is a behavior change for the public `/groups/:group_id/members` endpoint: large automatic groups (e.g. trust-level groups) that used to return up to 200 members by default now only return 50, which can break any existing API consumers or UI relying on the previous default page size, without any changelog/doc update reflecting this change.

isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard likely never true for spawn-context processes, so .kill() is silently skipped

_ensure_processes_alive() now only calls process.kill() when isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is true. Processes here are created via self.mp_context.Process where self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context('spawn'); such a call returns an instance of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which is a sibling of (not a subclass of) the generic multiprocessing.context.Process class that multiprocessing.Process refers to. Consequently this isinstance check evaluates to False for real spawned subprocesses, meaning the unhealthy process is never killed before _create_process_for_shards spawns its replacement. In join(), the for-loop over self.processes.items() does `break` when the join deadline has passed for the *current* process index. If multiple shards (now split across different per-process buffers) map to the same underlying Redis node, that node's ServiceMemory will be reported and summed multiple times, inflating 'used'/'available' totals used to decide spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage backpressure. Any existing custom/third-party implementation of this SPI (e.g. a custom grant type extension) will now fail to compile/deploy until it implements this new method, since no default implementation is provided. Given this is meant to be an extensible SPI (the PR description explicitly states "provider adds ability for someone to introduce his own provider"), this is a breaking change for existing extensions without a deprecation/default-method migration path.

`initToken()` now always runs the generated token id through `TokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId()`, changing the shape of the `jti` claim for every access token from a plain UUID to a prefixed value like `onrtac:<uuid>`. Any external tooling, logging/correlation systems, or internal code (admin REST API, introspection consumers, custom SPI implementations) that assumes the access token id is a canonical UUID (e.g. checks length 36, applies UUID regex, or compares it against other UUID-shaped identifiers) will now break. There is no configuration flag/toggle shown to disable this new encoding for backward-compatibility, and no migration note is provided for deployments relying on the previous token id format.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

Previously bleveBackend.BuildIndex held cacheMu.Lock() for the entire function (including running the builder callback that populates the index), which serialized all builds. This PR removes that lock and only takes cacheMu briefly at the very end to insert into b.cache. getOrCreateIndex() in search.go checks GetIndex() for a cached entry and, if absent, calls build()/BuildIndex() -- there is no synchronization preventing two concurrent callers for the *same* NamespacedResource key from both seeing a cache miss and both calling BuildIndex concurrently. For disk-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold), two goroutines would call bleve.New(dir, mapper) on the same directory concurrently, which can fail or corrupt index data; for memory-backed indexes, the loser's bleve.Index is simply overwritten in the cache map and never closed, leaking resources. The intended optimization (finer-grained locking) should still serialize builds per-key (e.g., per-key mutex/singleflight) rather than removing the serialization entirely.
